This manual offers generalized troubleshooting procedures for common types of malfunctions which can be appiled to most video games. We wil! not attempt to give you specific Instructions for troubleshooting particular games because thls would Involve hundreds of pages of more repetitive Instructions, differing only In the specific detalls of each game,
The most common problems occur in harness components such as the coln acceptor, player controls, Interconnecting wiring, etc. These areas are covered In moderate detall.
The TV Monitor and Game Logie Printed Circult Boards (PCB's) provide their fair share of problems too, but not to the extent of the harness and. I+s component parts.

As you already know, the Game Logie PC Boards are complex devices. Each contalns a great number of different Interrelated circults. The major changes which give each game Its own particular Individuality are accomp!Ished In the EPROMS and other Intigrated CIrcult devices that are Installed on each of these PC Boards.

The first step In troubleshooting Is to correctly Identify the malfunctions symptoms, This Includes not only the clrcults or features malfunctioning, but also those stI!! operational. A carefully tralned eye wil! pick up other clues to what's wrong as well. For [n= stance, a game in which the computer functtons fal! completely just after money was collect= ed may have a quarter shorting the PCR traces. Often an experienced troubleshooter will be able to spot the cause of a problem even before opening the cabinet,

After all the clues are carefully considered, the possible malfunctioning areas can be narrowed down to one or two good suspects. Those areas can be examined by a process of el|mination untl! the cause of the malfunction Is d!scovered.
Typical problems falling In thls category are coin and credit problems, power problems, and failure of Individual! features,

NO GAME CREDIT - ~ For example, a prospective game player Inserts a quarter or token and Ts not awarded a game, The first thing to check [s whether or not the quarter or token [s returned. {f I+ was returned, the malfunction most certainly !tles In the coln acceptor Itself, First, use a set of test colns (both old and new) to ascertain that the player's coln Is not undersize or underwelght. If your test coins are also returned, coin acceptor serv- Ictng Is Indicated. Generally, the cause of this particular problem |s a matadjusted magnet gate. Normally, this will mean slightly closing the magnet gate by turning the adjusting screw out a bit.

{¢ the quarter or token Is not returned and there Is no game credit, the cause of the mal~ function may be In one of several areas. First, try operating the coln return button; If the coln Is returned, the problem Is most !Ikely In the magnet gate. Enlarge the gap ac~ cording the coln acceptor manufacturers service procedures. (tf this does not cure the problem, remove the coln acceptor, clean It, and perform the manufacturers suggested major ad— justment procedure.

!f the trapped coln Is not returned when the wiper lever is actuated, you may have an acceptor jammed by a slug, gummed up with beer, a jammed coin chute, or mechanical fallure of the acceptor mechanism. In this case, first check for the stug that wll! genera!!y be trapped against the magnet. tf a slug Is found, simply remove It and test the acceptor. {f the chute Is blocked, remove the acceptor and remove the jammed coins. If there Is actual failure of the acceptor, remove the unlt and repair as Indicated by the acceptor manufacturers service procedures.

!f the cotn Is making Its way through the acceptor (that Is, falling into the coln box), yet there Is stil! no game credit, you elther have a mechanical! fallure of the coln switch or electrical fallure of the coln and credit circults. The first place to begin Is by checking the coln switch. Most of these switches are the make/break variety of micro switch, They are checked for continulty between the "NO", "NC", and "Ct terminals, When not actuated, the "NC" and "C" terminals shou!d be continuous and the "NO" terminal open. When actuated, the "NO" and "C" terminals should be continuous and the "NC" terminal open. If the coin switch checks good, Inspect the solder connections to the coin switch terminals to be sure there Is good contact at this point. If necessary, use a continulty tester and check from the terminal Jug on the switch to the assoclated PCB trace. This wil! tel! you if there Is a continuous |!ine al! the way to the cred!t clrcult.
lf the colIn switch wires do check good, the problem Is In one of the game !ogic boards - = most likefiy In the coln and credit cIrcultry.

tf you do get a game credit when a coin Is deposited, but the game wil! not start when the one or two player start button Is pressed, there may be a problem In the start switch, the Interconnect!ng wiring, or the game logic boards. First, check the switch, If the switch Is OK, proceed to check the wiring. Again, make sure you go from the termina! tug on the switch to the PCR trace. This way, you wllf check the terminal contact as wel! as the PCR edge connector contact. If the wiring Is continuous, proceed to check the PCB credit cir= cuit. If not, check each section .of the wiring, untii the discontinuity Is located. If the wiring ts OK, the problem must !le In the games logic boards.

Your game MUST have the correct IIne voltage to operate properly. If the |Ine voltage drops too low, one of the games logic clIrcults will disable the credit acceptance circult. The point at which the games logic cIrcults wi!! fall to function Is approximately 105 volts AC.

Low line voltage may have many causes. LIne voltage normally fluctuates a certain amount during the day as the total usage varles, Peak usage times occur malnty at dawn and/or dusk. So If your games problem seems to be related to the time of day, this may be a factor, A large load connected to the same !Ine as the game (such as a farge alr cond!tioner or other device with an exceptionally large electric motor) may drop the IIne voltage s!gnificantly when starting up. ThIs drop can result In an Intermittent credit problem, In addition, poor connections In the locatlon wiring, plug, or !!ne cord may also cause a signiflcant drop In power. Cold solder joints In the games harness, especially In areas !ike the transformer connections, Interlock switch, or fuse block, may a!so produce the same re~ sults, although probably on a more permanent basis.

Sometimes location owners (especially In bars) replace IIght switches with dimmer rheostats, and the game Is sometimes on the same IIne, Obviously, the voltage avallable to the game js going to drop dramatically when the dimmer 1s turned down.

In any case, the way to check for proper |Ine voltage ts with your VOM, Set the VOM to the 250 VAC scale and stick the probes Into the wal! outlet the game was connected to. If It's OK here, check the transformer primary connections. {tf you do not get 117 VAC, examine the solder joInts on the transformer, fuse block, and Interlock switch. If you do get 117 VAC, the problem must be elther In the transformer, harness connections, or In the PCB power supply.

\# you suspect the transformer, check Its secondaries with the VOM set to the 50 VAC scale and correlate the readings with the legend on the side of the transformer, The transformer must also be correctly grounded, so check the ground potentia!t as well, especlatly If there 1s a hum bar rolling up or down the Monitor screen.

NO POWER, NO PICTURE - - If the Monitor screen Is completely dark, first look in back of the Monitor to see If the CRT filament Is glowing. [{f It Is, try adjusting the brightness control. {tf no luck here, put your ear near the Monitor and IIsten for the high-pitched B+ hum produced by the flyback transformer. If you get the hum but no picture, and you have tried adjusting the brightness, major Monitor servicing Is Indicated.

{# the monttor seems completely dead, check the rest of the game to see !f It has power, If It doesn't, go directly to the wall outlet and check there. If OK there, check the game fuse(s), Interlock switch, and Interconnecting wire lengths.
Sometimes It Is difficult to tell If a slow=blow fuse has blown. {tf In doubt, check It us- Ing any of the VOM "R" scales.

HARNESS PROBLEMS - ~ Other harness problems Include blowIng fuses and matfunction!Ing controls, The repeating blown-fuse problem can sometimes be quite exasperating to solve. Short cIrcults have the tendency to occur In areas almost Impossible to find. First, try Insert- Ing a new fuse as old fuses age and sometimes hlow without cause. If the new fuse also blows, you definitely have a short.

The best way to approach thls problem Is by d!sconnecting devices that may be caus!Ing the problem, such as the TV Monitor, the varlous PCB's one at a time, and the Isolation trans~ former. Disconnect the devices by FIRST turning the game off, disconnecting It from its wall outlet. Remove the blown fuse and connect your VOM across the terminals of the fuse block (this wil! save blowIng a fuse each time you want to check the cIircult). Set your VOM to one of Its resistance scales. You should be reading a short. If not you probubly have a part that only shorts out after It Is heated up ~ we'l! cover this Im a minute. So, assuming you are reading a short on your VOM, disconnect the components from thelr cabling one at a time, checking the VOM after each one Is disconnected. When the short disappears, you have just disconnected the bad component. {f al! components are disconnected and the short still remains, the problem Is In the harness and only patient exploration wil! reveal its focation. Carefully examine all the wiring, looking for terminals that may be touching, metal objects such as colns shorting the connections, or burned Insulation, if necessary, use the VOM to check each suspected wire.

OK, now lets assume that you connected your VOM across the fuse block terminals as stated above and you did not read a short. This most !lkely means that you have a component somewhere In that game that ONLY goes bad AFTER it heats up. {+t checks good when Its cold. In thts case, turn the game off and disconnect ALL of Its components. Insta{il a known good fuse In the fuse block. And turn the game on. If the fuse does not blow after a tew minutes, you know that It Is not anything to do with the wire harness. (In this Instance, It shouldn't be, actually, Aut It never hurts to check.) Next, turn the game off again and reconnect ONE component, Turn the game back on and wait a few minutes to see If the fuse blows, If It does not, turn the game off again and reconnect another single component,

Turn the game back on and walt a few minutes to see If the fuse blows. Repeat thls procedure unti! the fuse blows. When I+ does blow, the last component you connected has the part on it that Is golng bad after It warms up and Is shorting out.
